turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): The N3 was a car park this morning. Was it as bad coming in from your side?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I wasn't counting the cars. I'm on my lunch, can we start.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Go on then. What's brought you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The hand goes dead on me at night. And I dropped a cup this morning, smashed it all over the kitchen. That's the reason I'm here.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dead, as in numb, or is it sore?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Numb. Umm, pins and needles in the thumb, the index and the middle finger, right hand mostly, and the left only if I lie on it. It's been about four months, since February.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waking you from sleep?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Every night nearly, two or three in the morning. I have to shake the hand to get it going again. I barely sleep and I'm wrecked the next day, so don't tell me I look tired.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't. The cup, is the grip going in the daytime as well?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Well actually the phone as well, a mug at the desk yesterday, and the cup this morning. The grip just goes and the thing is on the floor.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the hand with it, or only the numb feeling?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. Just dead and tingly. I already said numb.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry. Pain in the neck, or does it shoot down from the neck?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neck's grand.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any numbness in the feet?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Feet are fine.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Short of breath, or chest tightness when you're walking about?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I'm not here about my chest.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Give me the ordinary life in one go, would you, the job, the hours, the food, exercise, drink.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm in the office at the furniture factory in Navan, accounts, on the computer the whole day, hours half seven till half four, five days, and the odd Saturday if the invoices pile up. Diet is sandwiches at the desk and a takeaway most evenings, and a fry on the Sunday, and I don't exercise, the walk from the car park is the height of it. Four or five pints of a Friday, well actually it's four, and I don't smoke. There, happy?
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): That'll do. In the family, diabetes, blood pressure, heart trouble, any of that?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, my other sister is grand, and another sister has pressure but no sugar. I haven't got sugar myself, if that's the next question. Can you look at the hand.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): In a second. What tablets are you on?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, two tablets, if the hand is at me in the morning, not every morning. I was on naproxin five hundred milligrams twice a day for the hand and I stopped it in March, it did nothing and it turned my stomach. Amitriptaline got mentioned and I never took it, not once.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): So paracetamol when you need it, naproxen stopped since March, amitriptyline never started. Any vitamin or blood pressure tablet hiding in the press?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. That's the lot. Are we examining or chatting.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Examining. Both hands on the desk.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): They're there. The right is the one, obviously.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thenar bulk is preserved both sides, no wasting. Grip is a little weaker on the right than the left.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): What's thenar even mean.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Err, pad of muscle under the thumb. It's not shrunk, that's the good bit. Tell me what you feel when I tap the right wrist.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah that's the buzz, yeah. Don't keep doing it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Positive Tinel's on the right. Left wrist, no tingle when I tap. Light touch is duller on the right thumb, index and middle finger than on the ring finger.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. I could have told you the fingers. Are you done.

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Done with the hands, err, let me think this out loud. Little finger is spared so I'm not chasing the ulnar nerve, but night waking, the three fingers and the positive tap, my leading thought is the median nerve squeezed at the wrist, carpal tunnel, and I am not concluding it today. A root in the neck could still do this, and off sugars or a lazy thyroid can copy the whole picture. I will not put a final name on it yet.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): After all the poking you still don't know. For god's sake.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I know what leads the list and what I won't cross off. Let's see what the tests say before anyone stamps it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. So what do I actually do.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Get a neutral wrist splint off the chemist and wear it on the right hand at night for the next two weeks. It stops the wrist folding up in your sleep. You can still shake it out if it goes dead, but the splint is the thing that might settle it.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): A splint in the bed. I'll look an eejit. The invoices won't do themselves either if I'm messing about with appointments.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): The lads don't need to see it, it's for the night. Bloods are booked, not a maybe. The nurse takes bloods Thursday morning, fasting glucose and a thyroid test. Nothing but water from midnight, in at half 8, and you eat straight after.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday, half 8, fasting. I'll tell them at the office. This is eating my week.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): If those are borderline we do the third test, the B12. I'm not booking that unless they come back borderline.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): And the nerve test, is that today or what. Someone said nerves.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it does not settle with the splint, then we do nerve conduction studies. Conditional, not arranged.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it's the neck you were on about?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it does not settle, a scan of the neck, only in that case. I'll see you in two weeks with the bloods either way, that visit is booked.

spec.situation: Middle-aged office or factory worker with night-time numbness in thumb, index and middle fingers, shakes hands to wake them; dropping cups; splint advice, nerve test conditional.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

omissions.text: Daytime loss of grip is more detailed than recorded: patient dropped the phone as well as a mug at the desk yesterday and a cup this morning.
Amitriptyline was mentioned but the patient never took it, not once.
Family history detail omitted: mother did not have diabetes, and another sister is well.
Doctor explicitly noted the little finger is spared, supporting median rather than ulnar nerve involvement.
Blood tests were stated to be already booked with the nurse for Thursday morning at half 8, not just planned generally.
Follow-up was stated to be booked in two weeks with the blood results either way, not merely a general planned follow-up.
